title: A Northwestern Concentration Puts Quantum Computing On The Transcript
excerpt: Northwestern University now offers students a path to a quantum computing transcript as Illinois builds a quantum workforce.
content:
Computer Science majors at Northwestern University can now indicate their quantum expertise directly on their transcripts with a new concentration requiring four courses. The program aims to clarify a field often perceived as science fiction. According to Nikos Hardavellas, professor of Computer Science and Electrical and Computer Engineering, “a few lectures are often enough to spark real interest.” Northwestern is also building expertise across all levels by launching a quantum research track for PhD students, a strategic move to bolster the quantum industry’s long-term growth and talent pipeline.

Northwestern Launches Quantum Concentration for Computer Science Undergraduates

Northwestern University’s new Quantum Concentration requires completion of at least four courses from a curated list to earn the credential, a structure designed to visibly signal quantum expertise on a Computer Science graduate’s official transcript. The program’s accessibility is enhanced by a deliberate emphasis on mathematical foundations. linear algebra and programming fundamentals are the primary prerequisites, rather than advanced physics knowledge. Hardavellas notes that students engage with the subject surprisingly easily once introduced.

This initial spark is then nurtured by access to real-world quantum hardware; companies have donated computing time allowing students to run and test their code remotely. This addition, spearheaded by Hardavellas alongside colleagues Kaitlin Smith and Aravindan Vijayaraghavan, builds expertise across all levels of computer science education. PhD students on this track will complete coursework spanning theory, algorithms, computer systems, artificial intelligence and human-computer interfaces.

Quantum PhD Track Focuses on Systems and Information Foundations

Northwestern University’s new quantum track for doctoral students builds on a focused undergraduate concentration, offering a specialized path within the Computer Science PhD program. This addition allows students to deepen expertise while maintaining the broad foundation expected of all computer scientists, a strategic move for cultivating a workforce prepared for emerging quantum technologies.

Students entering the track will complete an array of courses spanning theory, algorithms, computer systems, and artificial intelligence, alongside two core quantum courses designed to bridge fundamental concepts with practical application. The curriculum emphasizes hands-on experience with real quantum systems, allowing students to assess algorithmic tradeoffs and explore future applications.

Foundational Quantum Course Enrollment Shows Consistent Annual Growth

This growth indicates a sustained interest in quantum education beyond introductory exposure, as students progress from initial curiosity to dedicated study. The course now draws a diverse cohort, with 19 graduate students and 14 undergraduates participating in the same sessions, alongside similar numbers in systems and applications courses. Completion of just four courses, including Quantum Systems, Quantum Computer Applications and Programming, Algorithms and Quantum Mechanics, earns the concentration, providing a concrete credential for prospective employers.

Students Envision Quantum Computing as Complementary, Not Replacement

The new Quantum Concentration at Northwestern University will appear directly on computer science majors’ transcripts, signaling a formalized commitment to quantum expertise beyond elective coursework. Options include Foundations of Quantum Computing and Quantum Information, Quantum Systems, Quantum Computer Applications and Programming, Algorithms, Quantum Mechanics and FPGA Design for Quantum Control. The core curriculum extends beyond theory, covering hardware modalities like superconducting and spin-based systems, alongside the challenges of noise, error correction and the quantum software stack. Nikos Hardavellas notes that students are often surprised by the overlap between classical and quantum computing.
